topics.title: Fungible Token Covenant Specification (KCC20)
topics.summary:
A draft specification called KCC20 was proposed to establish shared covenant standards for fungible native assets on Kaspa following the Toccata hard fork. Community members discussed how to handle advanced features like minting and freezing while keeping the core interface minimal.

This discussion lays the groundwork for native token interoperability and wallet support on Kaspa.

This proposal aims to enhance Kaspa's NFT capabilities by introducing covenant features and atomic batch transfers, supported by a functional mainnet demo.

topics.title: Permissionless Covenant-Based Prediction Markets – High-Level Sketch
topics.summary:
A community member proposed a high-level design for permissionless, covenant-based prediction markets using the KCC token standard, where participants mint paired YES and NO tokens and vote on outcomes after maturity.

It outlines a potential new utility for Kaspa's covenant system to support decentralized prediction markets and tokenized voting mechanisms.

history.what_happened: A community member proposed a new way to create open, community-run betting games—called prediction markets—where anyone can ask a question, set an end date, and let people trade "yes" or "no" tokens. To make sure winners always get paid, the system requires an equal number of both tokens to be created at the start, and relies on token holders to vote on the correct outcome once the event ends. While relying on voters isn't foolproof, the group agreed that adding reward incentives could encourage people to vote honestly and make the system work smoothly.

topics.why_it_matters: It outlines a potential new utility for Kaspa's covenant system to support decentralized prediction markets and tokenized voting mechanisms.

topics.title: Covenant tokens are the only Kaspa token type still missing metadata
topics.summary: Kaspa community members discussed how "covenant tokens" are currently the only type of Kaspa token missing basic information like a name, logo, or decimals, making them look blank on tracking apps. To fix this, developers have proposed a new standard called KCC-0021 that lets creators attach names, images, and symbols to these tokens right from the start. This solution keeps the underlying technology clean while making it much easier for everyday users to actually recognize and view their tokens on apps and marketplaces.

topics.title: Exploring a trust-minimized KRC-20 to KCC-20 bridge on Kaspa without relying on a relayer
topics.summary:
Crypto builders were discussing how to securely move tokens between different parts of the Kaspa network without having to trust a middleman. Someone suggested using smart contract "covenants," but the main roadblock is that Kaspa's base network cannot currently read the off-chain ledger records needed to verify token balances. 

Ultimately, the discussion highlights that a fully trust-free bridge is currently blocked because the necessary proof systems (like ZK proofs or state checkpoints) aren't yet available on Kaspa to verify token transactions on-chain.

topics.title: KCC-02: Control Principal References in Program ABIs
topics.summary:
Contributors proposed KCC-02 to standardize the concept of ownership and principal references within Program ABIs for covenants. Discussion focused on identifying principal roles, maintaining distinct identifiers for covenant lineages versus executable code, and ensuring wallets can verify on-chain state.

This standard is crucial for wallets and developers to reliably track ownership and control across both simple addresses and complex covenant programs.
topics.what_happened: Contributors proposed KCC-02 to standardize the concept of ownership and principal references within Program ABIs for covenants. Discussion focused on identifying principal roles, maintaining distinct identifiers for covenant lineages versus executable code, and ensuring wallets can verify on-chain state.

history.what_happened: The discussion focuses on how smart contracts should clearly define who "owns" or controls a digital token or asset, whether that owner is an individual person or another smart contract program. Participants suggested creating a standard way to list these owners so that crypto wallets can easily scan the blockchain and show users the assets they actually control. The group agreed that keeping different types of identifiers separate is important, and that wallets should always double-check the on-chain data to ensure security before confirming ownership to the user.

topics.why_it_matters: This standard is crucial for wallets and developers to reliably track ownership and control across both simple addresses and complex covenant programs.

topics.title: Kaspa as an immutable seal
topics.summary:
Community members are discussing a clever way to prove a document existed at a specific time and hasn't been tampered with, without actually uploading the private file to the blockchain. Instead, they use a unique digital fingerprint (or "hash") of the document and record it on the Kaspa network using a simple transaction. 

This matters because it offers a fast, incredibly cheap, and secure way to create permanent digital records and track official document updates over time.

topics.summary:
A community member suggested creating a "jury" of experienced developers and volunteers to review ongoing projects, help fix design flaws, and share useful knowledge. Another participant liked the idea in theory, but worried that auditing would take up too much time and energy, especially since many creators rely on AI tools and might not fully understand the underlying technology themselves. 

While the proposal highlights a strong need for better collaboration and catching missed opportunities, there is no final agreement yet on whether the benefits of a formal audit team would outweigh the heavy workload.

topics.title: Using Covenants for User verifications
topics.summary:
A developer asked if they could use the Kaspa cryptocurrency network to check a user's security clearance before letting them access special app content. Another community member replied that Kaspa is strictly designed for handling money, not for logging users in or managing security levels. 

The consensus is that you cannot use Kaspa as an authentication tool, meaning the developer will need to use a traditional login system for user verifications instead.
